title: Passive quantum memory in three dimensions
formal: Do there exist constants \(B,R>0\), a fixed finite inverse temperature \(\beta>0\), strictly increasing qubit counts \(n_j\to\infty\), local three-dimensional stabilizer Hamiltonians \(H_{n_j}\), and fixed encoding maps \(\operatorname{Enc}_{n_j}\), all satisfying the definitions below, for which \[\tau_{n_j}(\beta)\longrightarrow\infty?\] The dynamics couple every single-qubit Pauli error to the same specified positive-temperature bath, with no intervention during storage. This card retains a claimed affirmative resolution from May2026; the complete preprint proof has not been independently verified here.
definitions:
Place the \(n\) qubits at points in \(\mathbb R^3\), with at most \(B\) qubits in every closed unit ball. Each Hamiltonian is \[H_n=\sum_{a=1}^{M_n}\frac{I-S_a}{2}.\] The operators \(S_a\) are commuting, nonidentity Hermitian Pauli checks. Each has support contained in a ball of radius \(R\), and each qubit belongs to at most \(B\) checks. Support is the set of wires where a tensor factor is not identity. The common \(+1\) eigenspace of all checks must have dimension exactly two, so the Hamiltonian has a single encoded ground-space qubit. A check is a signed tensor product of \[I=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\quad X=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad Y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\quad Z=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},\] with overall sign \(+1\) or \(-1\). The coefficient of each term is fixed as displayed, so local energy penalties cannot grow with \(n\). The geometry need not be translation invariant, a regular lattice, or connected. The constants \(B,R\) work for the entire sequence. No efficient construction of the sequence is required.

All states live in finite-dimensional complex Hilbert spaces. A density matrix \(\rho\) is Hermitian, positive semidefinite and of trace one: \(\rho=\rho^\dagger\), \(v^\dagger\rho v\ge0\) for every vector \(v\), and \(\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1\). A quantum channel is a complex-linear map on matrices that preserves trace and is completely positive, meaning that its tensor product with the identity on every auxiliary register preserves positive semidefiniteness. Such channels model encoding, noise and recovery. Use units \(\hbar=k_B=1\), so physical temperature is \(1/\beta\). The same finite positive \(\beta\) is used for all sizes.

Here is the complete bath convention. Let \(\Pi_E\) denote the spectral projector of \(H_n\) at energy \(E\). For every site \(u\), every \(P\in\{X,Y,Z\}\), and every energy difference \(\omega\) for which the following operator is nonzero, define \[A_{u,P,\omega}=\sum_{E'-E=\omega}\Pi_{E'}P_u\Pi_E,\qquad g_\beta(\omega)=\min\{1,e^{-\beta\omega}\}.\] Thus positive \(\omega\) means an increase in system energy; its rate is suppressed by the Boltzmann factor. The generator on density matrices is \[\mathcal L_{n,\beta}(\rho)=-i[H_n,\rho]+\sum_{u,P,\omega}g_\beta(\omega)\left(A_{u,P,\omega}\rho A_{u,P,\omega}^\dagger-\frac{A_{u,P,\omega}^\dagger A_{u,P,\omega}\rho+\rho A_{u,P,\omega}^\dagger A_{u,P,\omega}}2\right).\] The commutator is \([H,\rho]=H\rho-\rho H\). The evolution for real \(t\ge0\) is the channel \(\Phi_{n,\beta,t}=\exp(t\mathcal L_{n,\beta})\), the finite-dimensional linear-map exponential. All single-site \(X,Y,Z\) couplings are included; no symmetry forbids one of them. Rates for allowed transitions are positive, and their attempt-rate normalization does not depend on size. The opposite-frequency ratio ensures the Gibbs state \(e^{-\beta H_n}/\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta H_n})\) is stationary. Although the spectral formula uses global energy projectors, commuting finite-range checks make these frequency components local: only checks meeting the site can affect its energy change. With the fixed range and density bounds, their support and possible energy changes are bounded independently of \(n\).

For each size choose one completely positive trace-preserving encoding \(\operatorname{Enc}_n\) from one qubit to the \(n\)-qubit system. It must have a completely positive trace-preserving left inverse \(D_{n,0}\), so \(D_{n,0}\circ\operatorname{Enc}_n\) is exactly the identity channel. This encoding may depend on the chosen temperature, and may initialize a thermal auxiliary state; it need not map entirely into the ground space or be efficiently preparable. It is chosen once for the device, independently of storage time and the unknown logical input. This retains the previous card’s thermal-encoding convention rather than adding a ground-state-only initialization requirement.

Let \(\|A\|_1=\operatorname{Tr}\sqrt{A^\dagger A}\) be the trace norm. For this fixed encoding define \[\varepsilon_{n,\beta}(t)=\inf_{D}\ \sup_{\rho}\left\|D\circ\Phi_{n,\beta,t}\circ\operatorname{Enc}_n(\rho)-\rho\right\|_1.\] The supremum ranges over every one-qubit density matrix; the infimum ranges over recovery channels \(D\) from \(n\) qubits to one. One recovery channel must work for every logical input at the given time. It may depend on \(n,\beta,t\), but cannot depend on the unknown input \(\rho\). Recovery is not required to be efficient. Define \[\tau_n(\beta)=\inf\{t\ge0:\varepsilon_{n,\beta}(t)>1/10\},\qquad \inf\varnothing=+\infty.\] The trace norm here has no factor of one half. Encoding occurs before storage and recovery only at readout; no syndrome measurements, feedback, cooling procedure or active corrections are allowed during the evolution. Divergence means that for every finite \(T>0\) there is an index \(j_0\) such that \(\tau_{n_j}(\beta)>T\) for all \(j\ge j_0\), at the same fixed temperature and local parameter bounds.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of existence of the family, fixed temperature and encoding maps in the displayed statement, including the lifetime bound for this generator, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation. The affirmative side need only prove divergence; a lower bound \(\exp(c n^\eta)\) for fixed \(c,\eta>0\) is stronger than required. The negative side must cover every admissible sequence and encoding, including thermal encodings, rather than a particular candidate geometry. The May2026 preprint claims a stronger affirmative bound, but this review has not independently verified its full construction or supplied its Lean formalization. A finite-size numerical trend or lifetime growth only up to a temperature-dependent crossover does not establish the fixed-temperature limit. Changing the bath with size, increasing local energy scales, forbidding local errors, adding corrections during storage, or demanding ground-state-only initialization changes the target.
why: A foundational question about whether quantum information can enjoy passive thermal protection in physical three-dimensional space. The recent claimed solution makes careful separation of storage, initialization, bath restrictions and stability especially important.

importance.reason: A defining problem at the intersection of quantum information and many-body physics; retained with an explicit claimed-resolution flag to preserve its history and prevent misleading open-status selection.

progress.text: Chesi and coauthors formulate thermodynamic criteria and relaxation bounds for stabilizer and subsystem quantum memories.
Brown and coauthors survey passive thermal memories, dimensional restrictions and proposed ways around them.
Stahl–Nandkishore prove symmetry-protected three-dimensional memory mechanisms with constrained dynamics.
The cored-product revision reports finite-size evidence on memories up to 60,000 qubits.
Balasubramanian–Davydova–Lin claim an affirmative solution with thermal encoding and stretched-exponential lifetime.
Williamson’s layer-code result appears in PRL; its guarantee is partial self-correction over a temperature-dependent size regime.

context_blocks.text: This record now has a claimed affirmative resolution. Balasubramanian, Davydova and Lin’s May 2026 preprint presents local three-dimensional stabilizer Hamiltonians with lifetime \(\exp (\Omega (n^{\eta}))\) at sufficiently low fixed temperature, for some \(\eta >0\). Its initialization is a thermal encoding. The catalogue flags this as a recent proof claim whose complete argument has not been independently verified here, rather than continuing to present the broad existence problem as confidently open.

A passive memory asks the Hamiltonian and its thermal environment to preserve information between an initial encoding and a final recovery. No repeated syndrome measurements or corrections are performed during storage. Quantum information requires preserving arbitrary superpositions, not only two distinguishable classical states. A material can preserve whether it is mostly magnetized up or down while rapidly losing the phase between those two possibilities; such a material is a classical memory, not a qubit memory.

The bath must be part of the mathematical specification. If errors that change the logical information are simply forbidden, a long lifetime may reflect that restriction. If every local transition is slowed as the device grows, a divergent lifetime can be manufactured by changing the clock. The generator above fixes the time scale and includes all single-qubit Pauli couplings, with ordinary positive-temperature suppression of energy-raising transitions.

An energy barrier is informative but does not alone determine memory time. A logical error may require crossing a high-energy configuration, yet the number of routes and intermediate configurations can be so large that entropy offsets the energetic suppression. Thermodynamic stability criteria therefore use both the bath dynamics and the thermal probability of configurations on which a recovery rule becomes unstable. A recovery map used to analyze the information is compatible with passive storage when it is applied only at readout.

The order of limits matters. Williamson’s layer-code result, published in August 2026, proves a regime in which lifetime grows exponentially with linear system size, but only up to a length scale exponential in inverse temperature. The lifetime at that crossover is very large as temperature falls. For the present question, however, temperature is fixed while system size goes to infinity, so an improvement restricted to a finite crossover regime is partial self-correction.

Roberts, Koh, Tan and Yao’s cored product codes take a different route using disordered geometry. Their January 2026 revision reports finite-temperature simulations of a pinwheel-based three-dimensional memory with up to 60,000 qubits, finding evidence that lifetime increases with size below a critical temperature. Those numerical results motivate a candidate construction but cannot by themselves establish the infinite-family limit required here.

Stahl and Nandkishore obtain protection in three dimensions by enforcing a one-form symmetry on the dynamics, even when enforcement is confined to a subvolume of vanishing relative size. This is a meaningful mechanism, but it restricts which local errors the environment may produce. The present model permits every single-qubit X, Y and Z coupling, so symmetry-protected results must be distinguished from this target.

The May construction’s proven version uses a randomized geometric embedding; its separate explicit variant lacks a complete lifetime proof. Efficient passive preparation and stability under arbitrary local Hamiltonian perturbations are also left for further work. These are additional requirements, beyond the fixed-Hamiltonian storage question formulated here.

The status distinction is useful for selecting research projects: the original existence target now requires assessment of the new theorem, while initialization, perturbation stability and alternative constructions remain separate directions. They should receive their own precise statements if added to the catalogue, rather than silently replacing the question under this identifier.

The current preprint’s Equation(5) prints a first-threshold condition with error at most \(1/10\), which already holds at time zero. The card instead defines lifetime by the first time the recovery error exceeds the threshold. The source’s substantive claim is the trace-norm estimate in Equation(3), supported by its stated stability theorem and §5.4; that estimate would imply the intended lower bound with this corrected convention.

sentences: Passive quantum memory aims to preserve an encoded qubit through the natural dynamics of a material without repeated active correction.
The question here fixes a nonzero temperature and asks whether lifetime can grow without bound in a three-dimensional local stabilizer system.
Protecting a qubit requires retaining phase information as well as distinguishing its classical basis states.
The saved card records a May 2026 claimed affirmative construction, while distinguishing its proof claim from an independently verified conclusion.
This makes the record a useful guide to the precise thermal model and remaining verification questions rather than an unqualified assertion that the original existence problem is still open.
